The polishing process was optimized to minimize roughness while simultaneously minimizing material removal. Two distinct polishing schemas were designed to remove partially melted particles from the surface and strike a balance between material removal and surface roughness reduction. Both schemas involved short-time polishing in the PEG electrolyte to remove partially melted particles, followed by transfer to the commercial solution for finish polishing. The primary difference between the two schemas lies in the duration of polishing in the commercial solution. The average starting roughness of the samples was Sa = 12.5 μm. Depending on the schema, the final roughness and material removal varied from Sa = 6.09±0.56 μm to 4.02±0.57 μm and ∆Z ≈ 9 μm to 240 μm, respectively (see Table 2). The average initial roughness was 12.36 μm +/- 1.82 μm, indicating that approximately half of the surface roughness is attributed to the presence of partially melted particles on the surface. The deviation down the length of a cylinder and across multiple samples was less than 10%, likely due to imperfect alignment of the sample and the counter electrode annulus, resulting in varied spacing between the two. However, the deviation between the two samples under the same schema was well within the deviation, demonstrating the repeatability of the process. The key difference between the two polishing schema is the mesoscale roughness, depicted as “waviness” in the figures below. The reduced waviness should minimize fatigue crack initiation sites, prompting the choice of schema 2 as the primary option. Overall, it was demonstrated that 316H SS can be polished, selectively remove particles from LPBF printed components, and do this repeatably through electrochemical polishing. Partially melted particles were successfully removed from the surface reducing the surface roughness UNCLASSIFIED AMMT – 316H SS Los Alamos National Laboratory Page 3-21 from 12.4 to 4.0 µm in 20 minutes, providing a rapid option for surface finishing complex shapes. Size Effect on Tensile Testing In many cases, customers may only have a limited amount of material available, which is insufficient to machine into full or sub-size tensile rods or dogbones as specified in ASTM or equivalent standards.
